content: White adipose tissue, also known as white fat, is one of the two types of adipose tissue found in mammals, the other being brown adipose tissue. In humans, white adipose tissue accounts for approximately 20% of body weight in men and 25% in women. The cells of white adipose tissue contain a single, large fat droplet that displaces the nucleus to the periphery, compressing it into a thin rim. These cells possess receptors for several key hormones, including insulin, growth hormones, norepinephrine, and glucocorticoids. The primary function of white adipose tissue is to serve as an energy reservoir. When insulin is released from the pancreas, it binds to insulin receptors on white adipose cells, triggering a dephosphorylation cascade. This cascade inactivates hormone-sensitive lipase, thereby inhibiting the breakdown of stored fat. Conversely, when glucagon is released from the pancreas, it binds to glucagon receptors on white adipose cells, initiating a phosphorylation cascade. This cascade activates hormone-sensitive lipase, leading to the breakdown of stored fat into fatty acids and glycerol. The fatty acids are released into the bloodstream, where they bind to albumin, while glycerol is freely released into the blood. Fatty acids are subsequently taken up by muscle and cardiac tissue to be used as a fuel source, whereas glycerol is taken up by the liver for gluconeogenesis. In addition to its role in energy storage and mobilization, white adipose tissue also functions as a thermal insulator, helping to maintain body temperature.
